## Development validation

This vignette accompanies development version 0.99.3.
The benchmark covers selected configurations, and the validation study uses
100 datasets per metric with 99 resampling draws. These small simulations
provide diagnostics; they do not establish general statistical calibration.
The refreshed local study observed 23% peak false positives, 10% peak
detection, 98.8% transfer prediction coverage, and 33% drift-fraction
coverage in the tested scenarios. Transfer intervals include response-noise
draws and can be conservative. These results limit inferential use of these methods. Report sources are `scripts/benchmark.R` and `scripts/validate.R`.

## Why optical spectroscopy needs its own statistics

Optical spectra are functions: a measured absorbance (or intensity,
reflectance, Raman shift) at each of hundreds or thousands of wavelengths.
The natural temptation is to run a pointwise t-test at each wavelength
and report the wavelengths where the p-value drops below 0.05. That
temptation is wrong. With 1000 wavelength bins and independent Gaussian
noise the analyst expects 50 false-positive wavelengths under the null at
`alpha = 0.05`. With positive autocorrelation across wavelengths the
false positives cluster, and the analysis produces spurious "regions of difference".

This vignette walks through three crossStatR functions that are designed
for optical data: `adaptive_smoothing()` for noise reduction with peak
preservation, `peak_evidence()` for assessing whether a candidate peak is
real, and `signal_difference_regions()` for identifying spectral regions
where two groups differ while controlling the family-wise error rate.

## Simulated UV-Vis-like spectra

The example simulates two groups of 12 replicate spectra each across 400-800 nm.
The "treated" group has an extra Gaussian absorption peak centred at
540 nm that is absent from the control group. Noise is correlated across
neighbouring wavelengths to mimic realistic spectrometer behaviour.

```{r sim-spectra}
set.seed(404)
wavelengths <- seq(400, 800, length.out = 200)
n_per_group  <- 12

make_curve <- function(group) {
  base <- 0.05 + 0.0006 * (wavelengths - 400)            # gentle slope
  peak1 <- 0.6 * exp(-(wavelengths - 460)^2 / (2 * 15^2)) # shared peak
  peak2 <- if (group == "treated")
    0.8 * exp(-(wavelengths - 540)^2 / (2 * 12^2)) else 0
  # Correlated noise: AR(1) across wavelengths
  e <- as.numeric(stats::filter(rnorm(length(wavelengths), sd = 0.06),
                                filter = 0.6, method = "recursive"))
  base + peak1 + peak2 + e
}

ctrl <- t(replicate(n_per_group, make_curve("control")))
trt  <- t(replicate(n_per_group, make_curve("treated")))
spec_df <- data.frame(
  wl = rep(wavelengths, times = 2 * n_per_group),
  absorbance = c(as.vector(t(ctrl)), as.vector(t(trt))),
  group = rep(c("control", "treated"), each = n_per_group * length(wavelengths)),
  rep   = factor(rep(rep(seq_len(n_per_group), each = length(wavelengths)), 2))
)

ggplot(spec_df, aes(x = wl, y = absorbance, group = interaction(group, rep),
                    colour = group)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Adaptive smoothing with peak preservation

Aggressive smoothing reduces variance but biases peak heights downward
and peak widths upward. The bias propagates: a smoothed peak height is a
downward-biased estimate of the true peak height. `adaptive_smoothing()`
makes this tradeoff explicit by minimising leave-one-out PRESS over a
candidate grid of Savitzky-Golay windows and vetoing any window that
shrinks the global maximum by more than 5%.

```{r smoothing}
example_curve <- trt[1, ]
sm <- adaptive_smoothing(wavelengths, example_curve,
                         method = "sgolay", poly_order = 3L)
print(sm)
```

The reported `peak_height_loss` is the fraction of the global maximum
lost to smoothing. If it exceeds 0.05, the peak-preservation constraint
forced the function to pick a smaller window than PRESS alone would
suggest. Inspect `press` and `peak_height_loss` together; if both are
large the analyst has a noisy signal with a sharp peak, and the analyst should consider
fitting a model to the raw data instead.

```{r plot-smoothing, fig.cap = "Raw and smoothed spectra. The smoothed curve follows the raw data closely at the peak, at the cost of slightly more residual noise."}
plot_df <- data.frame(
  wl = rep(wavelengths, 2),
  absorbance = c(example_curve, sm$smoothed),
  what = rep(c("raw", "smoothed"), each = length(wavelengths))
)
ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = wl, y = absorbance, colour = what)) +
  geom_line() + labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Absorbance") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Peak evidence: is the candidate peak real?

Given a candidate peak location, `peak_evidence()` reports a Gaussian
likelihood-style score and a resampling tail fraction. The score and
resampling procedure are exploratory: local simulations found poor null
calibration and low detection rates. Neither output establishes a calibrated
false-positive probability for a detected peak.

```{r peak-evidence}
pe <- peak_evidence(wavelengths, example_curve, method = "lr",
                    n_perm = 500, seed = 1)
head(pe$peaks, 5)
```

The score assumes a known noise SD and uses the baseline-subtracted
candidate amplitude. Resampling retains a smoothing spline, shuffles its
residuals, and compares a different local-contrast statistic with that
amplitude. The candidate set is not re-detected within each resample.
The resulting tail fraction requires methodological validation before
confirmatory use. Overlapping peaks also require a joint signal model.

## Simultaneous confidence bands for curve differences

To ask *where* the two groups differ while controlling the family-wise
error rate, use `signal_difference_regions()`. The function builds
pointwise t-statistics `\hat d(x) / s(x)` and replaces the pointwise
critical value with the `1 - alpha` quantile of the maximum absolute
t-statistic under the null (Westfall and Young, 1993). The null distribution is
estimated by a Westfall-Young permutation scheme: group labels are
exchanged between replicate curves and the max-t statistic is recomputed
for each permutation.

```{r sdr}
sdr <- signal_difference_regions(
  x = wavelengths,
  y1 = ctrl, y2 = trt,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  method = "max-t",
  n_perm = 500,
  seed = 1
)
print(sdr)
```

The reported `regions` data frame lists the contiguous wavelength
intervals where the simultaneous band excludes zero. The function also
returns the per-wavelength difference, the standard error, and the band
endpoints so the analyst can plot the band itself.

```{r plot-sdr, fig.cap = "Pointwise mean difference (black), 95% simultaneous confidence band (grey ribbon), and the identified significant region (shaded). Pointwise 95% intervals would include zero across most of the spectrum, falsely narrowing the apparent difference."}
band_df <- data.frame(
  wl = sdr$x_grid,
  diff = sdr$diff,
  low = sdr$band_low,
  high = sdr$band_high
)
# Mark identified regions
regions_df <- sdr$regions
if (!is.null(regions_df) && nrow(regions_df) > 0) {
  regions_df$ymin <- min(band_df$low)
  regions_df$ymax <- max(band_df$high)
}
p <- ggplot(band_df, aes(x = wl, y = diff)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Wavelength (nm)", y = "Mean difference (treated - control)") +
  theme_bw()
if (!is.null(regions_df) && nrow(regions_df) > 0) {
  p <- p + geom_rect(data = regions_df, alpha = 0.15,
                     aes(xmin = start, xmax = end, ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                     inherit.aes = FALSE, fill = "tomato")
}
p
```

## What simultaneous bands provide that pointwise tests do not

A pointwise 95% interval at each wavelength has 95% coverage *at that
wavelength*. It does not have 95% coverage for the *whole curve*. With
200 wavelength bins and independent Gaussian noise the probability that
at least one pointwise interval excludes zero under the null is roughly
`1 - 0.95^200 \approx 1`. The family-wise error rate collapses.

A simultaneous 95% band controls the probability that *any* point on the
band fails to cover the true difference, across the whole curve. The analyst can
report "the two groups differ in the region 525-555 nm" with the family-
wise error rate at the nominal level. Pointwise tests support no
such claim; they describe each wavelength in isolation.

The cost is power. A simultaneous band is wider than the corresponding
pointwise interval at every wavelength. The Westfall-Young permutation
adjustment recovers some of that power by accounting for the correlation
structure across wavelengths, which the Bonferroni adjustment does
not. With `n_perm = 0` the function falls back to a Bonferroni-adjusted
critical value, which is conservative; with `n_perm > 0` it uses the
permutation distribution, which is more powerful when neighbouring
wavelengths are correlated (as they almost always are in optical
spectroscopy).

## When the method fails

The permutation exchangeability assumption requires the two groups to
have the same noise structure. If the treated group has variance twice
that of the control, the permutation null distribution is wrong and the
band is too narrow. Inspect the group SDs across wavelengths and, if
they differ substantially, use `n_perm = 0` (Bonferroni) instead, or
apply a variance-stabilising transform before calling the function.

Region boundaries are limited by the grid resolution; sub-grid
localisation requires interpolation and is not done here. For very large
grids (>1000 points) the Bonferroni adjustment becomes extremely
conservative; permutation is strongly recommended.

## What to take away

For optical spectroscopy: smooth only when the analyst must, fit models on raw
data when the analyst can, and never report pointwise tests across a spectrum
without simultaneous-band control. `signal_difference_regions()` gives
the band and the regions; `peak_evidence()` indicates whether a
candidate peak is real; `adaptive_smoothing()` documents the bias it
introduces.

## References

- Savitzky, A. and Golay, M. J. E. (1964). Smoothing and Differentiation of Data by Simplified Least Squares Procedures. Analytical Chemistry, 36, 1627-1639. [Source](https://doi.org/10.1021/ac60214a047).

- Westfall, P. H. and Young, S. S. (1993). Resampling-Based Multiple Testing: Examples and Methods for p-Value Adjustment. Wiley. [Source](https://www.wiley.com/en-gb/Resampling-Based+Multiple+Testing%3A+Examples+and+Methods+for+p-Value+Adjustment-p-9780471557616).
